en: The Sūtra on the Fields of Merit Spoken by the Buddha, translated jointly by the Śramaṇas Fali and Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
Surrounded by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, ten thousand bodhisattvas, and countless others, he was preaching the Dharma.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with thirty-two thousand sons of the gods of the desire realm, each leading an incalculable retinue, came to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves upon the ground and sat down to one side.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, observing that the assembly was seated, received the Buddha’s divine intention, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I wish to ask a question; I only pray that you will graciously expound it, so as to provide a guiding rule for the world!”
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
“It is like a dark chamber; if one does not seek a lamp, how can anything be seen?
Excellent is your question!”
"I shall explain this to you in detail.
The Heavenly Lord addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a person plants virtue and seeks its reflected blessing, could there be such a fertile field where the retribution is limitless—that by planting even a hair’s breadth of the root of virtue, one obtains immeasurable merit?"
"I only pray that the Celestial Honored One will propagate your compassionate instruction, so that this ignorant one may receive immeasurable merit and retribution!
The Celestial Honored One sighed in praise, saying:
"How excellent, O Lord of Devas!"
The Dharma you have asked about is unsurpassed!
Listen attentively and reflect well;
I shall expound it in full for you, so that you may rejoice.
The Great Assembly of the Lord of Devas received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha addressed the Lord of Devas:
"Within the Sangha, there are five pure virtues that are called 'fields of merit' (puṇyakṣetra)."
By making offerings to them, one gains merit and may advance to Buddhahood. What are these five?
First, generating the aspiration to leave secular life and cherishing the Way within one's heart.
Second, they destroy their physical beauty in order to wear the dharma-robes;
third, they sever their ties of affection forever so as to be free from favoritism or aversion;
fourth, they cast aside their very lives in order to follow all that is wholesome.
Fifth, they aspire to seek the Mahāyāna because they desire to deliver sentient beings.
By virtue of these five qualities, they are called fields of merit;
they are excellent and beautiful, and they do not perish prematurely.
"The merit gained from making offerings to them is difficult to describe with a simile!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Having altered one's appearance to maintain the will and integrity, Severing attachments so as to have no worldly kin,"
Leaving home to propagate the holy path, vowing to deliver all people;
with five virtues transcending worldly affairs, they are called the supreme field of merit.
By making offerings, one attains eternal peace; such merit is foremost and most honored.
The Buddha told Śakra, Lord of Devas:
"Furthermore, there are seven kinds of extensive giving called 'fields of merit. The practitioner who performs them gains merit and is reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
What are these seven?"
First, to establish Buddhist stūpas, monastic quarters, halls, and pavilions;
second, to provide gardens with fruits, bathing pools, and trees for cool refreshment;
third, to constantly bestow medicine and treat all manner of illnesses.
Fourth, he constructs sturdy ships to ferry people across;
fifth, he establishes bridges to help the weak and frail cross over;
sixth, he digs wells by the roadsides so that those who are parched with thirst may drink.
"Seventh, one constructs latrines and provides facilities for the convenience of defecation.
These are the seven matters by which one attains the merit of Brahmā.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Building stupas and establishing monasteries, giving gardens and fruit for refreshing coolness,
relieving the sick with medicine, crossing people over with bridges and boats,
digging fine wells on desolate roads— those parched and weary find rest through these deeds."
Those born shall partake of ambrosia, free from illness and ever at peace;
by constructing latrines and providing cleanliness, one removes filth and attains lightness and joy.
Hereafter, there will be no suffering from defecation, nor shall one behold anything foul or evil.
"Just as the five rivers flow day and night without ceasing, so too is this merit;
in the end, one shall ascend to the Brahma Heaven.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Tiñcung (Śrutiśrava), who, hearing the Dharma, was filled with joy. He immediately rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The true Dharma of Buddhism is vast and its benefits immeasurable. Why is this so?
I recall that in the past, during countless lifetimes, I was born in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī as the son of an elder.”
By the side of the great road, he built a small vihāra and provided beds, bedding, drinks, and provisions for the community of monks;
those traveling who were exhausted from their journey could also find rest there.

By virtue of this merit, at the end of his life he was reborn in heaven as Śakra, Lord of the Devas; subsequently descending to the human world, he became a Cakravartin King. He did so thirty-six times in each realm, presiding over gods and men. Hair grew from the soles of his feet, and he traveled by treading upon the void. For ninety-one kalpas, his enjoyment of blessings was spontaneous.

Now that we have encountered the World-Honored One, who looks down upon all sentient beings to cleanse our ignorance and turbidity and settle us with pure wisdom, the roots of birth and death have withered; he is called a True Person (Arhat), and it is indeed thus that his blessed retribution is most true!
At that time, Tingcong recited these verses:
"Reflecting upon past lives, my offerings were slight;
Yet through the retribution received over distant kalpas, The remaining merit has allowed me to meet the Heavenly Teacher."
"Pure wisdom severs birth and death; delusion and attachment are eliminated without remainder.
The Buddha’s grace flows on without end; for this reason, I again take refuge.
At that time, Tingcong performed his prostrations and returned to his seat.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu named Bakula who rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I recall my past lives; I was born in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī as the son of an elder."
At that time, there was no Buddha in the world; however, the community of monks was teaching and transforming beings, holding a great assembly to preach the Dharma. I went to listen to the sutras.
Hearing the Dharma, I was filled with joy and took a medicinal fruit called harītakī, which I offered to the assembly of monks.

Due to this karmic retribution, at the end of his life he ascended to heaven; when reborn in the world, he always dwelt in a position of honor and nobility, being handsome, heroic, and preeminent among the masses, remaining free from illness for ninety-one kalpas.

By the remaining merit of encountering the Buddha, his light guided me out of the darkness of ignorance; he bestowed upon me the medicine of the Dharma, whereby I attained arhatship—power sufficient to move mountains and wisdom capable of eliminating evil.
"Excellent! The retribution of merit is indeed the ultimate truth!
At that time, Bakula spoke in verse:
"The compassionate bounty moistens the withered; Virtuous deeds rescue one from suffering and affliction."
The roots of goodness from a single fruit have brought forth blessings that endure to this day.
The Buddha has bestowed the meaning of the True Dharma; through his teaching, we transcend the abyss.
The protection of the Noble Assembly is boundless; I bow my head to the Supreme Field of Merit.
Then Pukkusāti, having paid his respects, returned to his seat.
Another bhikṣu named Sūdhāya then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated himself, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have reflected upon my past lives; I was born in the kingdom of Vaiśālī as the son of a humble family."
At that time, there was no Buddha in the world, and the community of monks was engaged in teaching and transforming others.

I was then carrying some curd, intending to sell it in the market, when I encountered the monks holding a great assembly to preach the Dharma. I passed by and stood to listen; the words of the Dharma were subtle and wondrous, and upon hearing them, I felt great joy. I immediately lifted my jar of curd and offered it as a gift to the community of monks.
The assembly of monks offered prayers of blessing, and his heart was filled with even greater joy.

By virtue of this meritorious retribution, at the end of his life he was reborn in heaven; when he descended again to the human world, his wealth and resources were limitless, and for ninety-one kalpas he remained noble, honored, and illustrious.

Due to the remaining karmic transgressions from his final life, he was born into this world; after his mother had been pregnant for several months, she fell ill and passed away, and he was buried within her tomb, only to be born when the full term of the pregnancy had reached its end.
For seven years within the tomb, she sustained herself by drinking the milk of a deceased woman.
Through the power of a slight merit, she encountered the Buddha; he opened and elucidated the luminous Dharma for her, enabling her to transcend the realm of death and attain the state of an Arhat.
"How true! How real are sin and merit;
it is exactly as the Buddha has taught! At that time, Sudāya spoke in verse:
"Formerly I was the son of a humble family, Selling curd to sustain myself."
With joyful exultation, though giving but a meager gift, one attains liberation from the afflictions of the three sufferings.
Though born within a tomb of sin and sustained for seven years by drinking milk, through these very conditions one attains deliverance; I take refuge in the Noble Field of Merit.
At that time, Sudāya, having paid his respects, returned to his seat.
Then another bhikṣu named Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I recall my past lives: I was born in the kingdom of Rājagṛha as the son of a commoner. My body was afflicted with a malignant ulcer that would not heal despite treatment."
A friend who was a practitioner of the Way came and said to me:
"You should bathe the assembly of monks and take that bath water to wash your wound; it will then be healed, and you will also gain merit!"

I was immediately filled with joy and went to the monastery, where I increased my reverence and devotion. I had a new well constructed and prepared bathing implements with fragrant oil; I bathed the assembly of monks and used the resulting water to wash my sores, whereby they were soon healed.

Due to these causes and conditions, he was born with a handsome appearance, his golden complexion radiant and bright, free from any dust or impurity; for ninety-one kalpas, he constantly attained pure merit, and his protection by the Sangha was vast and far-reaching.
"Now, having again encountered the Buddha, the defilements of my mind have been extinguished, and I have attained arhatship.
Before the Buddha, Ānanda spoke in verse:
"The Noble Assembly is like a skilled physician, Rescuing and relieving those afflicted by suffering and distress."
By bathing and offering purity, his sores were healed and he attained peace.
His appearance was always upright and handsome, with a complexion more exquisite than purple gold.
His virtue was moistening and boundless; I take refuge in this excellent field of merit.

After Ānanda had prostrated and returned to his seat, there was at that time a bhikṣuṇī in the assembly named Nairañjanā. She rose from her seat, adjusted her robes, paid homage, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall my previous life, when I was born in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī as a poor woman."
At that time, there was a Buddha in the world named Kāśyapa, who was then surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma. I was present in the assembly;

hearing the sutra, I rejoiced and desired to give alms, but looking around, I found I had nothing. Reflecting on my own poverty and low station, my heart was moved with sorrow. I went to another’s orchard to beg for fruits and melons, intending to offer them to the Buddha.
At that time, he obtained a single *nālikera* fruit, large, fragrant, and beautiful; carrying a bowl of water along with the one fruit, he offered them to Kāśyapa Buddha and the assembly of monks.
The Buddha, knowing her sincere intention, accepted it with a prayer of blessing and distributed the water and mangoes so that they reached everyone everywhere.
By virtue of this merit, when her life ended, she was reborn in heaven and became the Queen of Heaven.
Descending to be born in the world, he did not do so from a womb; for ninety-one kalpas, he was born within the *nāgapuṣpa* flower, upright and pure, always conscious of his past lives.
"Now that we have encountered the World-Honored One, he has opened and revealed the eye of the Way.
At that time, the daughter of Na uttered these verses:
"The compassion and moisture of the Triple Gem are universal; In the perfection of wisdom, there is neither male nor female."
By giving fruit as a great gift, one gains the conditions to leave behind all sufferings.
Born amidst flowers in this world, one may even become a Queen of Heaven;
by taking refuge in the protection of the Noble Assembly, one’s field of merit becomes most profound and deep.
After the bhikṣuṇī Nairañjanā had paid her respects and returned to her seat,
the Lord of Devas rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One:
"In a previous life, I was born in the great kingdom of Kuru as the son of an elder."
Carried by a maidservant in blue robes, he entered the city to sightsee and encountered a multitude of monks begging for alms in the streets and alleys.
Seeing that there were many people giving offerings, he thought to himself:
"How would it not be a joy to obtain wealth and treasures to bestow as alms upon these monks!"
He immediately untied his pearl necklace and gave it as an offering to the assembly of monks.
With one mind they offered prayers for him, and he departed with joy.

By virtue of this cause and condition, at the end of his life he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as Śakra, Lord of Devas; for ninety-one kalpas, he remained forever free from the eight difficulties.
Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of Devas, spoke in verse:
"Virtue so sublime, none can surpass; The source from which blessings flow and calamities are blocked.
By the power of the Sage’s assembly and divine concentration, Even the young are moved to joy."
“Emulating the joyful giving of the multitude, you have transferred your spirit to preside over the two heavens.
Having taken refuge in the World’s Most Benevolent One, I vow to serve the Honored One in every lifetime.
The Buddha addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the great assembly:
“Listen to what I say regarding my past conduct.

Formerly, in a previous life, I established a latrine by the side of a great road in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Among the people of the kingdom, there was none who, having attained ease and comfort, did not feel gratitude for this act of righteousness.”

By virtue of these merits, one’s birth shall be pure and clean; though practicing the Way through successive kalpas, one will remain unstained by defilement. With great merit fully perfected, one shall spontaneously attain Buddhahood.
"The golden body is radiant, with dust and water failing to adhere; food is digested of its own accord, free from the affliction of excrement.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Enduring impurity while cultivating meritorious deeds, One remains unsullied by others."
By constructing latrines and providing facilities for ease, one attains lightness and tranquility from heavy burdens.
This merit eliminates arrogance; through it, one understands the conditions of birth and death, advances toward the path to Buddhahood, and becomes a sublime, empty, and pure Honored One.
The Buddha told Śakra Devendra:
"Among the ninety-six kinds of paths, the path of the Buddha is the most honorable;
among the ninety-six kinds of teachings, the teaching of the Buddha is the most true."
Among the ninety-six kinds of monastic orders, the Buddha’s Sangha is the most correct. Why is this?

Because from incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) past, the Tathāgata made vows with sincere truth, sacrificing his life and accumulating merit, vowing for the sake of sentient beings to practice giving—whether it be national treasures, wealth, wife and children, head, eyes, blood, or flesh—without a heart of attachment or craving.

If the mind is like empty space, covering all things without exception; if the six perfections, the four immeasurables, and all manner of virtues are universally complete; and if wisdom and merit are fully perfected, one then attains Buddhahood. One’s body shall be the color of purple-gold, with marks and signs beyond compare;
there is nothing in the past, future, or present that is not illuminated and understood. Among the honored deities of the three realms, none can equal such a being;
their words are trustworthy and their virtue so profound that they cause heaven and earth to tremble.
If there are sentient beings who give rise to even a single thought of reverence toward the Tathāgata, they shall obtain a greater reward than the treasures of a great trichiliocosm!

He expounds the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and the twelve divisions of the sūtras, distinguishing between transgressions and blessings with utter sincerity. He opens the teachings of the three vehicles so that each may practice them accordingly; those who hear him rejoice, delighting in becoming śramaṇas, believing in the Buddha and practicing the Dharma, their aspirations noble and pure.

Within the community of monks, there are the four pairs and eight types of noble ones, the twelve worthy ones; having abandoned worldly greed and strife, they guide the world and open the way to merit, ensuring that the paths for devas and humans remain open—this is the source of the Sangha.
This is the most honored, unsurpassed Way; from it all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats emerge, transforming and teaching all, delivering and liberating all living beings.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, the assembly of Śakra, Lord of Devas, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and incalculable numbers of people attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Thereupon, Ānanda knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?"
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The name of this sutra is 'The Field of Merit for All Virtues. You should always uphold it, clearly proclaiming its teachings, and ensure that it does not suffer any deficiency."
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the assembly of Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the entire congregation were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
Thus ends the *Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Fields of Merit*.
